analysis.one_liner: Lets the government use Superfund money to assess and recover damages for natural resources destroyed by oil and chemical spills.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was sent to four House committees and died there, with the House noting its subject was being handled in a separate oil pollution bill.
analysis.plain_summary: After a string of major oil spills in 1989, including Alaska, this bill would let federal and state officials use Superfund money to measure the damage that oil and hazardous-substance spills do to fish, wildlife, and habitat. Any money recovered from the companies responsible would have to be spent putting those resources back or buying equivalent ones. It would also require new federal rules for valuing that damage, which the bill's findings said current rules badly undervalue.
analysis.who_benefits: People who depend on healthy coasts, rivers, and fisheries — commercial and recreational fishermen, coastal communities, and the public generally. Taxpayers also benefit from a polluter-pays structure: the money spent on damage assessments would come from the Superfund (which is financed by industry excise taxes), and money recovered from responsible companies would be dedicated to restoring the damaged resources.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the legal ban on using the Superfund to pay for federal and state natural resource damage assessments, which the bill says currently 'seriously impedes' those assessments and lets polluters escape restoration responsibility [S3].

Requires that every dollar recovered from polluters for natural resource damage be kept by the trustee and spent only to restore, replace, or acquire the equivalent of the damaged resources [S2] [S3].

Directs the President, acting through NOAA and in consultation with EPA and the Fish and Wildlife Service, to issue regulations within two years governing how damage to natural resources from oil and hazardous-substance releases is valued [S2] [S3].
Responds to the 1989 spills in Alaska, Delaware, Texas, and Rhode Island, which the bill says risked severe damage to fisheries, marine mammals, and endangered species and their habitat [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and chemical companies and other parties responsible for spills and hazardous releases, who would face government damage assessments and be liable for the full cost of restoring destroyed fish, wildlife, and habitat. Superfund money spent on assessments would also draw on the industry-financed trust fund.

drawbacks.text: Damage assessments for natural resources are expensive and contentious; requiring new valuation rules and litigation could take years and consume Superfund money that would otherwise fund actual site cleanups [S3].
The bill locks recovered money exclusively into restoration, replacement, or acquiring equivalent resources, giving trustees no flexibility to direct funds to other pressing cleanup needs [S2] [S3].

Placing a dollar value on fish, wildlife, and habitat is inherently imprecise, and companies would contest the assessments, likely producing lengthy disputes over the required regulations and individual recoveries [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: polluters would pay to restore natural resources they destroy, rather than the public absorbing the loss. The main cost is that assessments cost money and time, and some of it comes from a cleanup fund — but the bill's premise is that without funded assessments, polluters escape responsibility entirely. On balance the trade favors the public, though the valuation process would have invited dispute and delay.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees and bounced among subcommittees, never got a hearing or vote, and died at the end of the Congress — with the House formally noting that its subject was being handled in a separate oil pollution bill, H.R. 1465.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 28, 1989, by Rep. Gerry Studds with no cosponsors, and referred jointly to four committees: Merchant Marine and Fisheries, Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Public Works and Transportation [S1] [S2] [S4] [S5].

It was then referred to multiple subcommittees, including Transportation and Hazardous Materials, Water Resources, and Fisheries and Wildlife Conservation and the Environment, and executive comment was requested from the Commerce and Interior Departments and EPA [S5].
On August 3, 1989, the House recorded 'See H.R. 1465,' indicating the bill's subject matter was being pursued through that separate oil pollution bill [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill and no floor vote ever occurred; it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and hazardous-substance polluters were better off that this version never advanced, since it would have funded assessments and locked recovered money into restoration. However, Congress did enact a broader oil pollution law later in the Congress through H.R. 1465 (widely reported), so the biggest provisions of this idea were not entirely lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Polluters avoided this version's liability provisions

for.name: Rep. Gerry E. Studds
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MA), sponsor; chairman of the Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with no cosponsors and chaired the primary committee of referral, which never reported it.

against.name: House committees of referral (Merchant Marine and Fisheries, Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Public Works and Transportation)
against.role: Committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill to the floor; it was passed among subcommittees and died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: One Democrat sponsored the bill with zero cosponsors and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan pattern appears in the record.

industries.note: Would face funded government damage assessments and liability for the full cost of restoring fisheries, wildlife, and habitat harmed by spills. Its cost is the public's gain under a polluter-pays structure.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and hazardous waste generators
industries.note: Hazardous-substance releases into natural resources would trigger the same assessment and restoration liability, financed in part by the industry-funded Superfund trust.
